The one-pager (2026-10-14): fill-in leave-behind for the partner/principal who was not on the call

STPi — the one-pager (for the person who wasn't on the call)

Send this when a prospect says "I need to ask my partner / principal / spouse." That person never felt the call's emotion — they only get logic. So this page is built for them: the owner's own numbers, one payback line, one safety paragraph, one exit. Print it, WhatsApp it, or paste it into an email. Replace every [bracket] with the prospect's own numbers from the call (sales-scripts-emotion.md §3). If you don't have their numbers, don't send the page — book the 10-minute numbers call instead.

[Owner name], [practice/agency], [town] — STPi in one page

The problem, in [owner]'s words: "[their anger quote, verbatim]" Today the hunt-and-rewrite takes ±[N] hours a week. At [owner]'s rate that's ±R[X] a month spent typing — and every new candidate makes it heavier.

What STPi does: It hunts country-specific sources (keys and availability vary) across South Africa, Zimbabwe and Zambia twice a day, Monday–Saturday, scores every ad against each candidate's real profile, and drafts a tailored cover letter + country-formatted CV. Each one arrives as a card. [Owner] taps ✅ to send or ❌ to delete. Nothing is ever sent without that tap — there is no automatic mode. The writer may only use facts already on the candidate's profile; it is forbidden from inventing experience, and drafts delete themselves after 72 hours.

The maths (conservative, [owner]'s own figures): - Typing removed: ±[N] hrs/week ≈ ±R[X]/month of billable time back. - Cost: Solo $306/month (about R4,999) — 3 candidates, 100 sends/month. - Payback: one CV-and-letter bundle sells for R600–R1,500; one placement is worth [R fee]. [One placement covers ±[ ] months of STPi.] If it doesn't earn its keep, it should be cancelled — and can be, in two clicks.

Safety, in one paragraph: Applications go out from your own mailbox, signed as the candidate, capped at 20 per candidate per day so the mailbox stays clean. Candidate data lives in a file you own — delete the file and it's gone. No LinkedIn login, no profile scraping, no data sold or shared.

How starting works: The demo is free forever (1 candidate, full pipeline) — no card. Setup takes ~10 minutes on a call; the team does it with you. Paid plans run month-to-month on Whop; annual is 25% off by bank wire. Mukuru/EFT and Lightning are accepted for ZA/ZW buyers.

The decision we'd like: [ ] Run the free demo on one candidate this week [ ] Start Solo ($306 (about R4,999)) [ ] Talk again on [date] Contact: [seller name, WhatsApp]

Numbers marked "±" are [owner]'s own estimates from our call on [date], not STPi claims. Prices: USD billed on Whop, rand figures approximate.

copy/emotional-scorecard.md 535 words

Emotional scorecard & pre-call Diagnosis (2026-10-14): 10-point call scoring, Diagnosis sheet, emotion funnel metrics

STPi — emotional scorecard & pre-call Diagnosis

Companion to emotion-engine.md. Score every sales call within an hour of hanging up. Review three scored calls a week. A call that "went well" but scores under 6 will come back as "let me think about it" — find which emotion never fired and drill that stage.

The scorecard (1 point each)

# Checkpoint ✓
1 Prospect said the typing/hunt is the bottleneck in their own words
2 We agreed the enemy out loud (06:00 queue / 40 tabs / speed beating quality)
3 Prospect gave their hours/week and hourly rate — their cost number exists
4 Asked "12 months of nothing changes?" and heard "worse" (or their version)
5 Prospect named their bench: how many candidates wait without a pipeline
6 Prospect said what they'd do first with the hours back (verbatim noted)
7 Demo ran the three scenes in order: card/letter → coverage/caps/purge → their maths + the tap
8 Prospect was invited to audit letter vs CV for an invented fact
9 Price was framed against one placement / bundle — never "per month" alone
10 Close quoted their own words (recap) and ended in silence + a dated next step

Score bands: 9–10 close or a clean no. 6–8 stalled deal — re-ignite with the missing emotion (sales-scripts-emotion.md §7). ≤5 polite death — requalify the prospect list, not the script.

Pre-call Diagnosis (5 minutes, before any call/demo)

Prospect: ______________________  Type (solo/studio/agency/centre/NGO): __________
Evidence found (2+ signals, cold-outreach-emotion-rotation.md): _________________
Their public promise (their words): ____________________________________________
Likely dominant emotion (anger / fear / greed): _________________________________
Their enemy, named: ___________________________________________________________
Estimated typing cost: ±___ hrs/week × R___ = ±R______/month (CONFIRM on call)
One placement / bundle is worth: R________  →  covers ±____ months of Solo
Safety proof they'll need most (tap / no-invention / caps / purge / Sovereign): ___
Who else decides (partner/principal/spouse): ____________________________________
Opening line (one true, specific sentence): ______________________________________

Funnel metrics (add to whatever you already track)

  • Evidence rate — outreach sent with real research vs generic. Generic should trend to 0.
  • Scene completion — demos that reached Scene 3 (their maths). Below Scene 3, price talk is premature.
  • Close-on-call rate — demo set up (or tier sold) before hanging up.
  • 72-hour first-card rate — first card landed within 3 days of setup. This is the churn-killer; chase it operationally.
  • 7-day upgrade nudge reply rate — by archetype; tells you which greed currency your market actually wants.
  • 30-day refund/cancel rate — your manipulation detector. If emotion outruns truth, this rises first. When it moves, re-read emotion-engine.md §8 before touching any script.

Weekly 30-minute review

  1. Pick 3 calls (one won, one stalled, one lost). Score them.
  2. Name the weakest stage across all three. Rewrite exactly one script line for it.
  3. Check one number above. If first-card rate slipped, fix onboarding before writing more outreach.

BRAND.md 402 words

The brand file — voice, phrases we use and never use

STPi — brand & voice

Palette

Name Hex Use
STPi #27548f Logo stroke, buttons, links, highlights
Charcoal #2B2B2B Body text, wordmark on light
Lilac tint #eef4fb Backgrounds, cards, table stripes
White #FFFFFF Canvas
Green (approve) #1E8E3E ✅ moments only
Red (reject) #B00020 ❌ moments only

Type

Wordmark: Poppins / Montserrat 600, tight tracking (-1.5 at display sizes). Body: any clean sans (system stack is fine). Never a serif for UI copy.

Logo files (in brand/)

File Use
stpi-logo.svg / .png Default on light backgrounds
stpi-logo-white.svg On stpi / charcoal
stpi-logo-mono.svg Single-colour print, invoices
stpi-logo-on-navy.png Dark heroes
stpi-icon.svg, stpi-icon-512/192/32.png, favicon.ico Avatars, app icon, Telegram bot (use 512)
stpi-tile.svg Source for tiles / pattern
stpi.svg/.png "by Jacaranda Labs" credit, footer, DPA
og-image.png (1200×630) Share card everywhere

Rules: minimum logo height 24 px; clear space = one magnifier-circle on all sides; never recolor the stroke outside the palette; never put the charcoal wordmark on a dark background (use white); never stretch.

Voice

  • Plain. Short sentences. Concrete nouns.
  • Specific beats impressive: "41 drafted applications, zero auto-sends" > "powerful AI".
  • Honest about limits: we say what it won't do (auto-send, invent, scrape LinkedIn).
  • The human is the hero. STPi is the tool. Never "our AI got her the job."
  • No emoji in email bodies except the ✅/❌ pair when literally describing the buttons.
  • Southern-African specifics welcome (SARS eFiling, SAIPA, NRC, EcoCash) — they signal we actually know the market.

Do / Don't

DO: lead with the card (it is the product). Lead with the tap (it is the trust). DO: price in the open; hosting cost is part of the pitch ($0, no card). DO: show the 72-hour purge and the 20/day cap unprompted — they answer the two fears every buyer has before they ask. DON'T: "revolutionise", "game-changer", "AI-powered future", "guaranteed interviews". DON'T: call it a bot in buyer-facing copy ("bot" reads as spam); "pipeline" / "copilot". DON'T: screenshot a real candidate's card — only the demo persona (Thabo is the example profile shipped in the repo).

downloads/pricing.md 575 words

Demo kit pricing sheet (ships inside the zip)

STPi — pricing (decided 2026-09-17, founder-approved mandate)

Currency: US dollars, set to the rand value (owner decision 2026-09-27: Whop bills USD; rand figures are approximate at R16.31 per $1). ZA/ZW/ZM buyers can also pay sats via Lightning or Mukuru/EFT at the day's rate. Bill monthly via Whop; annual = 25% off (the cash lever that funds the build); affiliates 30% recurring 12 months.

Tier USD/mo ≈ ZAR Candidates Sends Extras
Demo $0 forever R0 1 5/mo full pipeline, Discord card, PDFs, 72 h purge
Solo $306 ≈ R4,999 3 100/mo priority hunt slots
Studio $613 ≈ R9,999 15 fair-use (20/day/candidate guard-rail) white-label PDFs, brand header
Sovereign $920 ≈ R15,000 unlimited guard-rail self-hosted, onboarding day, data never leaves

Why these numbers

  • Demo R0/forever is the marketing budget. 1 candidate × 5 sends shows the whole loop (hunt → card → tap → send) without costing us anything: ~1 hunt-minute/day on Actions, cents of LLM on the customer's own key. The upgrade trigger is natural: the second candidate. "You upgrade when your bench asks" is the honest funnel.
  • Solo $306 (about R4,999) ≈ two-to-three bundled CV-and-letter sales at prevailing coach rates (R600–R1 500), plus the 8–12 h of hunt-and-rewrite it deletes. If STPi doesn't earn its keep the customer cancels in-app and is right to. Annual $2,754 (about R45,000, 25% off) is the prepay close — one deal ≈ six months of runway, cash now.
  • Studio $613 (about R9,999) is priced for throughput, not seats: a CV studio that triples writer output earns it back in one extra order a week. White-label is the wedge — studios sell their brand, so the PDF header carrying their logo is the feature they'll pay the jump for.
  • Sovereign $920 (about R15,000) undercuts one junior-recruiter-day and removes the two objections agencies actually have (data residency, vendor lock-in). Onboarding day included because self-host failures are support tickets; a guided day is cheaper.
  • Prices are USD at the rand value of the 2026-09-23 service-first memo tiers (owner decision 2026-09-27): Solo $306 / Studio $613 / Sovereign $920 monthly (about R4,999 / R9,999 / R15,000); annual 25% off. ZW/ZM buyers can pay sats via coinos or Mukuru/EFT at the day's rate. Billing is enforced fail-closed (stpi billing grant).
  • Affiliates 30% / 12 months because coaches talk to coaches; Whop runs it natively and 30% is the number that makes a coach mention you unprompted.

Lines to use verbatim

  • "The demo is free forever. You upgrade when your second candidate asks for it — that's the whole sales funnel."
  • "Solo is $306 a month (about R4,999) — two or three CV bundles at your rates, and the ten hours of typing is gone. If it doesn't earn its keep, cancel in the app, no retention call."
  • "Annual prepay is $2,754 (about R45,000) — three months free, one payment, provisioned same day."
  • "Sovereign costs less than a junior recruiter's Tuesday."

Never

  • Discount in public. Discount in private for: universities, NGOs, cohorts of ≥10 coaches.
  • "Cheap" as a selling point. The selling point is hours; the price is just not a barrier.
  • Per-send pricing. It incentivises spam and contradicts the 20/day guard-rail story.

OWNED PRESS — dev.to essay 1, full text (our best inbound asset)

I treat job applications as a pipeline, not a resume problem

Published on dev.to (owner persona), mirrored on Nostr. Archived here verbatim, fetched 2026-10-01.

Every piece of career advice still assumes the bottleneck is the document. Polish this, quantify that, beat the ATS parser with the right keywords. None of it disputes that the words matter. All of it ignores that most applications never reach a human because of where and when they were aimed, not what they said.

Here is the failure order I keep observing, roughly in order of damage:

  1. The role was wrong for you and you knew it, but a blank Sunday said otherwise.
  2. The application went out four to nine days after posting, into a pile of hundreds.
  3. The letter was generically excellent and specifically empty, so the reader felt the form letter.
  4. Only then, maybe, does a parser or a recruiter glance at the resume itself.

A CV tweak fixes item three at best. The real fix is operational: treat the search as a small production system with sourcing, screening, drafting and a quality gate. This post is about the one I built and run for other people, stpi, and specifically the architecture, because the architecture is the part worth stealing even if you never touch my code.

The nightly hunt

A scheduler (in our case free GitHub Actions, four in the morning local time) walks a configured set of sources: PNet, Careers24, PiH, the PSVAC government gazette, LinkedIn's public job search, and a few niche feeds. Each source is a scraper plus an adapter, because there is no other honest word for it: the gazette is unstructured PDF, one board blocks bots at the edge (which incidentally protects legitimate small pipelines from the four-hundred-application crowd), another returns RSS, another a JSON API pretending to be a website.

The interesting part is what happens on nights with zero results. Zero is not a bug report, it is market data: global remote boards genuinely rarely pay off for a Harare or Johannesburg profile, and a pipeline that measures that lets you stop taking it personally. We log every source's yield and it changes how people aim.

Scoring against a truth file

Every candidate role gets scored against two documents: the CV, and what we call the truth file. The truth file is a short list of verified facts: projects, dates, numbers, technologies, contexts. Its whole purpose is negative: the model may only cite what appears there. If it is not in the truth file, it does not exist for the application.

This is the single most underrated control in any LLM drafting system. Not tone, not temperature. Provenance. A drafter constrained to a truth file produces boring, checkable prose, and boring prose that survives a reference call beats confident prose that does not. Our scorer also learns, gently: when a candidate taps "no" on an approval card, the reason codes feed back into ranking, so the same category of bad fit comes back less often.

The queue, and the brake

Drafted applications land as interactive cards on Discord (or Telegram): role, company, salary if posted, the fit score with reasons, and a preview of the letter. Each card has exactly the actions you would want to exist: approve and send at the scheduled time, edit the draft, reject with a reason, snooze.

Nothing sends without a yes. That rule is not a disclaimer, it is the design. Every auto-apply product I have seen fails the same way: it optimises volume, reply rates collapse, sender reputations burn, and the human stops reading their own applications. A pipeline that sends on your behalf without a gate is not a job-search tool, it is a reputation destroyer with good marketing. The approval step is where your judgment enters the loop, and judgment is what the market actually pays for.

Caps are enforced in software, not in promises: candidates per night, sends per month, usage counters persisted on disk next to the state, and the machine simply stops and asks when a cap is hit. Demo builds get small caps; paid tiers raise them; nobody gets a surprise invoice from a runaway agent because runaway is not representable in the system.

Why it runs on your infrastructure

The whole thing is a Python package plus a repo with a scheduler. The data plane (CVs, truth files, queue state) lives in your GitHub repo or your own box; the only third party it talks to is the LLM provider you choose, and a failover chain of them, so one provider's rate limit does not starve a hunt mid-run. There is no account to make with us, no database of your candidates sitting on someone else's server, and when you stop paying, the pipeline keeps running because it was never hosted by us in the first place. That is also why payment is honour-based: the hosted service is convenience, the capability is yours.

What I would tell you to copy

If you would rather build your own, and honestly you should if this is your day job, steal the shape:

  • Measure source yield nightly and let zero-days retarget you.
  • Constrain the drafter to a provenance document. Boring beats brilliant.
  • Freshness beats fit: submit within hours of posting or do not bother.
  • Keep a human on the trigger and put the caps in code.
  • Log every rejection as training data; your no is smarter than your yes.
  • Run it where your data lives. Automation that needs you to trust a stranger's database will eventually give you a reason not to.

The machine is a small factory with one employee and one quality gate, and the gate is you. Everything else is plumbing, and the plumbing is the part you are allowed to buy.

OWNED PRESS — dev.to essay 2, full text

Six prompts that do the boring 80% of your job search (copy-paste)

Published on dev.to (owner persona), mirrored on Nostr. Archived here verbatim, fetched 2026-10-01.

Every job-search advice article argues about wording. Almost none of them argue about the actual bottleneck: the volume of reading, scoring, tailoring and following-up that sits between a job board and an interview. That part is language work, and language work is exactly what these six prompts are for. They are deliberately boring. That is the point: your judgment stays on the five decisions that matter, the machine carries the two hundred boring ones.

One rule before you start. These prompts are for the pipeline, not for the performance. Everything that leaves your name stays in your voice, edited by you. An interview measures you; a draft is just logistics.

1. The job description deconstructor

Read the following job description. Split it into: (a) the requirements they state, (b) the requirements they repeat or front-load, which are the real ones, (c) what this role is secretly for, inferred from team context, reporting line and the problems they describe, (d) the seniority this actually is, regardless of title. Be blunt about uncertainty. JD: [paste]

Most of the value here is (b). A description that lists "owns priorities" three times wants a different candidate than one that lists it never.

2. The honest fit score

Here is my CV and a job description. Score fit 0-100 against the REAL requirements you identified, and output: the top three evidenced matches with the CV line that proves each, the top two gaps, and a one-paragraph verdict on whether I should spend an application on this at all. Do not be encouraging. CV: [paste] JD: [paste]

The instruction that changes everything is "whether I should spend an application on this". Applications are not free; they cost the twelve minutes of tailoring and the emotional toll of the silence after. Score the role, not just the match.

3. The tailored one-page pass

Tailor my CV for this role. You may reorder, reweight and rephrase; you may NOT add experience, numbers, tools or employers that are not in my input. For every bullet you change, note which JD line it now answers. Keep total length to one page. CV: [paste] JD: [paste]

The "note which JD line it answers" trick does double duty: it gives you the tailoring and it gives you the interview prep material in one pass, because "why is this bullet here" is the second question every interviewer asks.

4. The three-sentence reach-out

Write a 3-sentence message from me to the hiring manager for this role, sent when the posting is fresh. Sentence one: the specific thing in the JD or their company's work that shows I did two minutes of reading. Sentence two: the single strongest evidenced match. Sentence three: a zero-pressure line about availability. No flattery, no "I hope this finds you well". Context: [JD + your one-line pitch]

Three sentences because hiring managers read these on a phone between meetings, and anything longer is instantly pattern-matched to mass mail.

5. The five-day nudge

Write a 40-word follow-up to my earlier application for [role]. It must add one new piece of information (a relevant result, a shipped thing, an answer to a question the JD raised) so it does not read as begging. Refer to my earlier message without apology.

Follow-ups with new information get answered; "just floating this" follow-ups teach people your name is noise.

6. The rejection post-mortem

I applied to [company/role] and got the standard rejection after [how long]. Write the two-sentence email that politely asks for one piece of specific feedback, targeted at the recruiter rather than the system, and phrased so that answering takes under a minute. Then list five patterns from my recent rejections (attached list) worth tracking.

You will get maybe one reply in ten. One reply is one datapoint, and five datapoints beat any career coach who has not seen your actual numbers. Keep the replies; they are the only ground truth in the whole pipeline.

The operating cadence that makes these work

Prompts alone just speed up bad habits. The boring 80% only pays when three operational rules ride along: apply within hours of a posting rather than days after polishing (a fresh average beats a stale perfect entry into a pile that grows by the hour), batch the pipeline reads into fixed windows instead of doom-scrolling, and keep one plain table of status for every live application so nothing rots untracked.

stpi is what it looks like when that cadence is the product instead of the habit: mailbox ingestion, scoring against the JD, tailored drafts behind a human approval gate, follow-ups on schedule, caps and cooldowns so the machine cannot send you into burnout. The demo is free and self-hosted. But the six prompts above run the honest version of this pipeline on nothing but a free LLM tier, and that is genuinely enough to change a month of searching. Your move on the other side of every draft still matters more than the tool. That part is not automatable and I would not trust anyone selling it.

The buyer pages — every word, verbatim

The pages a buyer or demo user actually reads, stripped to text (images become captions). Quoting from these is always safe.

HomeSetup guideDemo

in one inbox you already read, with a STPi alert when an employer answers. Operators and candidates both get

Paid feature: own-domain sending is available on Solo, Studio and Sovereign. Demo and the 7-day trial
use a Gmail app password and send from that Gmail; they cannot connect a domain or a non-Gmail mail server.
What employers seeLerato Dube (via Momentum Careers) <lerato.dube@momentumcareers.co.za>
Where replies goYour reply inbox (Cloudflare forwards the whole domain there), plus the candidate directly (Reply-To); STPi alerts the operator
Who sees sent mailCandidate receives a private Bcc copy; the operator has a Sent copy in Gmail/IMAP
Who signs the mailYour domain (DKIM through the relay), so Gmail and Outlook see a properly authenticated sender
CostRelay route: the domain only (about R100–R200/year for a .co.za); Cloudflare Email Routing and the relay free tier cost R0. If you already run a mail server, STPi can use its SMTP + IMAP at no extra email-provider cost.
1 Domain DNS
Buy a domain from any registrar (a .co.za is cheapest), or use one you already own.
For the relay route, put the domain on a free Cloudflare account and change the registrar's nameservers to the two Cloudflare shows. For your own mail server, keep your existing DNS provider and MX if you prefer.
Already have a mail server (for example, your own cPanel/Exim setup)? Keep its MX and skip Cloudflare Email Routing. Your server must accept mail to the candidate addresses (catch-all or aliases), allow SMTP sending with those From addresses, and provide IMAP for STPi's reply alerts. Use its own SMTP/IMAP login in section 2 and choose “My own mail server” in section 3. STPi will save sent copies through IMAP. No separate relay subscription is required. If your existing provider is Google Workspace or Microsoft 365, it must permit the candidate aliases as send-as addresses; otherwise use a relay.
2 Forward the whole domain to your Gmail (free)
In Cloudflare: your domain → Email → Email Routing → enable. Let it add its MX and SPF records.
Destination addresses → add your Gmail → click the link Cloudflare emails you.
Routing rules → Catch-all address → action Send to an email → your Gmail → enable.
Now anything@yourdomain reaches your Gmail, which is why STPi never has to create addresses one by one.
3 A free sending relay
Cloudflare only receives. To send as your domain, pick one free relay:
Brevo (recommended)SMTP2GO
Free tier / STPi safety cap300/day; STPi allows up to 140 applications/day including each candidate's private copy1,000/month; STPi allows up to 15 applications/day including each candidate's private copy
Add your domainSenders, domains & dedicated IPs → Domains → Add a domain → Authenticate. With Cloudflare, “authenticate automatically” adds the brevo-code TXT, the two DKIM records (brevo1/brevo2._domainkey) and DMARC for you.Sending → Verified senders → Add sender domain → add the CNAME records it lists in Cloudflare → Verify.
STPi needsSMTP & API → SMTP tab: the SMTP login (…@smtp-brevo.com) and a new SMTP keySending → SMTP users → add a user: its username and password
Paste the SMTP key, not your account password. Free tiers are for your own clients' applications,
one at a time after you approve them. That's exactly what STPi sends, so don't use the relay for newsletters or bulk mail.
4 Tell STPi
Hosted (Solo, Studio, Sovereign)
In your Discord workspace press 🔐 Connect. For Cloudflare Routing + a relay, section 2 is the Gmail (reply inbox),
then section 3 is domain + relay credentials. For a server you already run, choose My own SMTP/IMAP server in section 2,
enter its host/login/password, and select My own mail server from section 2 in section 3. STPi tests SMTP, IMAP and DNS,
then posts the results in your channel. If your server only supports SMTP port 465, choose 465; IMAP uses SSL port 993.
Self-hosted (Sovereign)
# tenant.yaml: the relay sends, your Gmail reads replies
mailbox:
provider: brevo                 # or smtp2go, or custom + host/port
address: applications@momentumcareers.co.za
username: 9a1b2c001@smtp-brevo.com
display_name: Momentum Careers
app_password: enc:...           # stpi encrypt <SMTP key>
inbox:
provider: gmail
address: you@gmail.com
app_password: enc:...           # stpi encrypt <Gmail app password>
sender_domain: momentumcareers.co.za
$ stpi sender-check momentum
✅ momentumcareers.co.za: ready
✅ Receiving: MX points to Cloudflare Email Routing (set a catch-all to your Gmail).
✅ SPF found.
✅ Brevo ownership code published.
✅ DKIM: relay signing key published.
✅ DMARC found.
lerato01             -> lerato.dube@momentumcareers.co.za
$ stpi mailbox-test momentum
Already have your own SMTP/IMAP server? No Brevo or SMTP2GO account is needed. In the paid hosted form choose
“My own SMTP/IMAP server” and “My own mail server from section 2”. In self-hosted tenant.yaml, use:
mailbox:
provider: custom
address: ops@momentumcareers.co.za
host: mail.momentumcareers.co.za
port: 465                    # implicit TLS; 587 STARTTLS also works
username: ops@momentumcareers.co.za
imap_host: mail.momentumcareers.co.za
imap_port: 993
app_password: enc:...        # encrypt the server's mail password
inbox: null                    # same server is the reply inbox
sender_domain: momentumcareers.co.za
Have your mail administrator verify catch-all/alias routing, “send as” permissions, SPF/DKIM/DMARC, and that IMAP login works.
If you only have a domain but no mail server, choose Cloudflare routing + a free relay instead.
5 Addresses
Automatic: first and last name, lower-case, accents dropped. Ruth Nyasha Mhlanga becomes ruth.mhlanga@, and Lérato Dube-Mhlanga becomes lerato.dube-mhlanga@.
Two clients with the same name, or a preference? Set send_as: ruth.m@yourdomain in that candidate's profile (self-host), or ask in your help channel (hosted).
When a client finishes, nothing to delete: the address simply stops being used. Mail to it still reaches you.
Replies are matched to the right person by the address they were sent to, even when an employer answers from a
different system with a new subject line.

  • Each board has its own employers and its own posting habits
  • Duplicates across boards are a signal the role is real and urgent
  • Coverage is a schedule problem: check the same boards at the same times every day
Follow-ups are where placements leak
follow-up-leak · short · audience: operator

Most agencies track applications sent; far fewer track which ones need a nudge this week.

  • A reply table per candidate: sent, followed up, replied, closed
  • A follow-up a week later often gets the reply the first send didn't
  • The table also tells you which boards and employers actually answer
A consultant's week, with the busywork taken out
consultant-week · short · audience: operator

When searching and drafting run on a schedule, a consultant's week turns into reviewing, coaching and closing.

  • Monday: approve the weekend's drafts in one sitting
  • Midweek: coaching calls and interview prep, the work clients value most
  • Friday: send the proof-of-work note and plan next week
Set the reply expectation on day one
set-expectations-day-one · short · audience: operator

Clients judge you on employer silence unless you explain, before the first send, how hiring timelines really work.

  • Tell them silence is normal and what a normal week of activity looks like
  • Agree what you will report and when
  • Clients who were told the truth on day one stay through a quiet month
Running a placement desk as a pipeline
placement-desk-pipeline · longform · audience: operator

Treat each candidate's search as stages with owners and timings, and the desk scales without heroics.

  • Intake: consent, one master profile, target roles and countries
  • Sourcing on a schedule across boards, with duplicates merged
  • Drafting and review: one approval pass per round, nothing sent unreviewed
  • Follow-up and reporting: the reply table and the weekly client note
How a small coaching practice grows without hiring
grow-practice-without-hiring · longform · audience: operator

The next hire is usually a response to busywork; remove the busywork and the practice can take more clients first.

  • Find the hours: audit a month of client work by task
  • Which tasks need your judgment and which only need doing
  • Package the service around outcomes clients can check
  • What to automate, what to keep human, and where the line sits

The promo card gallery

Every autopilot post ships with a card rendered in the runner for $0 (press/cards.py). Cards are built from editor-approved text only, so an image can never say something a post could not. Palette follows the topic — same idea, same colours on every rail — and the layout rotates between quote and points so feeds don't look stamped. Promo cards carry the price strip straight from live billing.

wide   1200x675   x, linkedin, bsky, nostrnote, whop_public, whop_private
pin    1000x1500  pinterest
cover  1000x420   devto, nostr30023 (dev.to crops covers to 1000x420)

Wide cards — one per promo topic (43)

Pins & covers (86)

The promo kit - 60 ready-to-post materials

Every entry is one promotional message in nine channel formats. 40 are text cards (wide for X/LinkedIn/Bluesky/Telegram/Facebook, pin for Pinterest) built from editor-approved copy; 20 are cartoon illustrations - hand-styled pictures with short captions, the art is the material. Copy passes the same editor gates as authored posts: one pointer link, prices exactly as billing writes them, no hype vocabulary. The autopilot takes the next unused material per rail before authoring anything; a rail that burns the kit falls back to authored promo. Rebuild with python3 press/promo_kit.py.

Sovereign in one file — docker-compose.sovereign.yml

# STPi Sovereign (self-hosted). Guide: https://getstpi.pages.dev/setup#sovereign
#   1. put this file and your .env in one folder (.env needs at least STPI_LICENCE_KEY + STPI_MASTER_KEY)
#   2. docker compose up -d
#   3. docker compose exec stpi stpi licence-status      -> should say OK
# The image is public; your signed licence (posted in your Discord after purchase) is what unlocks it.
# An expired or missing licence makes STPi read-only (dashboard works, hunting/sending stops).
services:
  stpi:
    image: ghcr.io/stpi-cloud/stpi:latest
    restart: unless-stopped
    env_file: .env
    environment:
      STPI_MODE: selfhosted
    volumes:
      - ./data:/data          # SQLite, drafts, PDFs
      - ./config:/config      # tenants/<firm>/tenant.yaml + candidates
    ports: ["8080:8080"]      # dashboard: http://localhost:8080 (sign in with STPI_ADMIN_TOKEN)

The landing FAQ — verbatim (what a buyer reads before deciding)

Why is the download not gated by an email form?

Because you'd delete our number the second the demo expired, and we'd rather you forwarded the ZIP. The demo runs entirely on your machine — we couldn't collect your data if we wanted to.

What happens to my candidates' ID numbers, emails, CVs?

They live in a YAML folder on your box or your private GitHub repo, and that's it. The product ships with a right-to-erasure button (delete file = gone, logs keep only an opaque id) and 72-hour PDF expiry.

Is the demo actually the product?

Bit-for-bit — one environment flag separates demo from paid (STPI_FLAVOUR=demo). No feature lobotomy, just a one-candidate / five-monthly-send allowance with no expiry and a lot of purple upgrade banners.

What's your licence stance?

Commercial, source-included, and each released version converts to MIT 24 months after release. The demo you're downloading may be freely re-shared unmodified — that's in the licence itself.

The landing page — verbatim copy (every word a buyer can read)

-- extracted 2026-10-09 from stpi/landing/index.html --
STPi — Strategic Talent Placement Infrastructure — find jobs, write the paperwork, send them. Free demo, no email needed
What it does while you sleep
Hunts PNet · CareerJunction · Careers24 · Bizcommunity · iHarareJobs · VacancyMail · JobsZimbabwe · GoZambiaJobs · UNjobs · Impactpool — per-candidate keywords, excludes and city prefs.
Drafts one LLM call per match: relevance score, cover letter, tailored CV — never invents facts, uses only the candidate profile you approve.
Renders print-ready PDFs (ZA/ZW/ZM CV formats) and sends the card: "Accountant @ Acme — Match 87%" with ✅ / ❌.
Only after your tap: it emails the ad's apply address from your mailbox, signed as the candidate, with the PDFs attached. Capped per candidate and per day so your mailbox never gets flagged.
When the employer answers: the reply reaches the candidate and you, and STPi pings you: interview invite, question, no, or a bounced address.
$ pip install ./stpi-1.0.1-py3-none-any.whl && stpi serve
✔ demo flavour active — one candidate · five sends per UTC month · free forever
$ stpi hunt --dry
✔ 11 new matches for lerato01 — top 5 drafted
⬆ unlock everything from $306/mo (about R4,999) — buy: https://whop.com/jacaranda-labs (demo nag, deleted on upgrade)
Run it free, forever… on your own terms
Zero infrastructure. The default deployment is two GitHub Actions workflows —
no server, no Docker, no credit card. Your state lives in your private repo.
Your keys, your mailbox. Bring a free-tier Groq/Cerebras/Gemini key and a Gmail
app-password for your sending mailbox. We never hold either; both are encrypted at rest on your box.
Nothing to leak. Server side you keep {job_url, status, timestamp}.
PDFs auto-purge in ≤72 h. No CRM, no tracking pixels, no "sales team will contact you".
Self-hosted option. Agencies that want sovereignty run the Docker image on their
own box with a signed offline licence (read-only when it lapses — never a bricked machine).
Buy it, board it, run it — no ticket, no waiting on a human
Half of software support is "where do I click now?". Here is the whole
journey, start to running, in one list. Every screen you'll open says the same things in fewer words.
Buy on Whop (store, plans below). Whop messages you
within a minute: your licence plus your personal setup link (/start/…).
Open your setup link. It asks for exactly the three things a machine can't guess —
your WhatsApp number (for licence delivery),
your Gmail app password (Google: 2FA on → App passwords),
and a free LLM key (Groq or
Gemini). Each field carries its own one-minute how-to.
Hunts start on the next cycle. Matches arrive on your dashboard as cards — ✅ sends, ❌
skips. Nothing emails without a tap, ever; send caps keep your mailbox reputation boring.
Add your own clients (candidates) in the same dashboard. The candidates page posts one card
per job seeker: ➕ Add types their details (attach their CV with /candidate add cv:),
🔗 Invite mints a private link you WhatsApp them — they fill in their own details, upload their CV and
give consent, and you approve before they're hunted. Plan seats (5 / 25 / unlimited) are the only ceiling.
Is it us or is it you? The machine answers for itself:
stpi-mint /health
— "ok": true and a fresh tick = everything is running; your screen is the place to look.
Need help anyway? Same-day human on WhatsApp — for outages, not onboarding.

Playbooks — tier by tier, channel by channel

Brand-safe operating plays per tier. Not new claims — every line traces to the pitch, the scripts, or the storefront copy in the Copy vault.

Solo — the independent coach

Who buys. One-person career coaches and job agents with 1–5 paying clients and a Sunday that dies in CV Word files. Not job seekers themselves — say so early, it saves both sides an hour.

The moment. They just lost a client to "I found one myself" or they just took client #3 and physically cannot hand-write three more tailored letters a week. Sell into that week.

The demo move. "Load your hardest current client into the demo tonight. One candidate, free forever. When the first approval card lands in your Discord, forward it to your client without comment." The card sells; you go quiet.

What Solo is. 3 candidates, 100 sends a month, priority slots, Discord approvals. Their mailbox, their name, their client sees their brand. Rands checkout exists; so does the $2754 annual wire (25% off) for the coach who hates subscriptions.

Kill shot. "You bill by the client, not by the hour. STPi is the only hire that works nights, never phones in sick, and asks permission before it acts."

Common stall. "I can do this with ChatGPT." True — and the six-prompt essay (Copy vault) literally teaches that. The counter: prompts don't hunt boards at 06:00 SAST, don't purge PDFs at 72 h, don't cap your sends so your mailbox stays out of spam. They are buying the ops, not the words.

Studio — the practice with a name to protect

Who buys. Coaching studios and boutique agencies: 2–10 consultants, a brand on the letterhead, clients who must never see a second-party logo.

The moment. The founder just hired consultant #2 and quality became a lottery. Or a client asked "where does my CV actually go?" and the answer embarrassed them.

The demo move. Same as Solo, then in the walkthrough open a sample PDF (Media vault -> samples) and ask whose name is on it. White-label PDFs are the Studio sentence that matters; say it once: "PDFs branded as your agency."

What Studio is. 15 candidates, fair-use sends, white-label documents, the LLM fallback chain (one provider outage never stops Friday's run). Rands at R9,999; annual wire at $5,517.

Kill shot. "Solo makes one coach faster. Studio makes five coaches look like ten — under one letterhead."

Common stall. "Per-seat pricing?" No. Per-practice. The counter: compare to one consultant's billable week, not to a SaaS seat.

Sovereign — the institution

Who buys. Institutions and agencies whose counsel asks data questions first: universities, outplacement firms, NGOs running workforce programmes, corporates with POPIA-sensitive employee data during restructures.

The moment. Procurement asked for the data-flow diagram and every SaaS answer ended in "trust us." Sovereign's answer fits in one sentence: your data never leaves your servers.

The demo move. Don't demo first. Send the architecture one-liner from the Engine tab plus the compose file (Demo kit). Let their engineer run docker compose up on a Tuesday afternoon; the signed licence arrives in their Discord after checkout.

What Sovereign is. Self-hosted Docker, unlimited candidates and sends, signed offline licence, install help in their private channel, lapsed licence = read-only, never bricked. $920/mo, R15 000 in rands, $8 280 annual by wire.

Kill shot. "You're not buying a subscription, you're buying the keys. If we vanished tomorrow your pipeline keeps hunting."

Common stall. "Self-hosted means maintenance." The counter: it is one compose file and a scheduler; upgrades are an image pull. They already maintain mail servers — this is lighter.

The upgrade staircase (sell the next tier before they ask)

Solo -> Studio triggers: the 4th candidate conversation, the "can the letter say our name" question, a second consultant joining. Studio -> Sovereign triggers: the compliance questionnaire, the institutional RFP, the data-residency sigh. Move people the week the trigger fires — the lifecycle mails (Copy vault) watch for it, the human closes it.

Channel plays — same truth, different rooms

X — opener is the card or the number, never the feature list; one CTA (the demo); 3+/day/persona; threads for the pipeline story, singles for proof. The six-prompt essay endlessly re-quoted beats any ad.

LinkedIn — the coach's-platform voice: slower, first-person, one lesson per post; the approval-card screenshot outperforms every polished graphic. Mandatory daily; company page + persona both.

dev.to — we do not market there, we teach. Essays and topic-driven how-tos; the only CTA lives at the end and it is the demo. 3/day across the two personas; per-persona author pages carry the trust.

Pinterest — visual proof only: pins from cards.py (card, boards, pipeline). Search traffic compounds; pin daily, forget the feed exists, check the digest monthly.

Nostr / Bluesky — niche, technical, zero ad-speak; mirror the essays, answer questions, leave. Daily presence, weekly value.

Whop public forum — the store's own front porch, 1/day: field notes from real runs, branded card images, trial /g/ links, and (once the owner flips it) the affiliate recruitment topics (see Storefront tab). Never copy-paste a social post verbatim here — the forum rewards shop talk, bills hype.

Whop paid (members) — not a billboard: onboarding notes, status, fairness. Members who feel informed renew; members who feel marketed at, refund.

The 8-week sprint: $10k/mo by 2026-12-09

Day 1 is Friday 2026-10-09. The deadline is Wednesday 2026-12-09 — 61 days, ~8.5 weeks. This is the only plan in this bible with a date on it, and the only one that is ordered: do the earlier thing before the later thing, every day. Nothing below requires budget, headcount, or product changes — only hours, in the right order.

The target, stated twice. (1) MRR run-rate ≥ $10k/mo by Dec 9 — recurring revenue, not vibes. (2) Cash collected along the way ≥ $10k — money in hand. Annual prepays count in full toward (2) and 1/12th toward (1). Both numbers come from the Whop dashboard, never from memory.

The arithmetic. Whop takes ~3% + processing, so $10k net means ~$10.5k gross. Any of these mixes clears it:

Mix Customers Gross/mo
Balanced: 3 Sovereign + 7 Studio + 12 Solo 22 $10,723
Studio-heavy: 17 Studio 17 $10,421
Whale: 11 Sovereign 11 $10,120

That is ~3 new paying customers per week, every week, for 8 weeks. The weekly number is the scoreboard — not traffic, not followers, not feelings.

The cash accelerator. One Studio annual ($5,517) plus one Sovereign annual ($8,280) is $13,797 cash from two deals. Every quote shows the monthly price first and the annual second (pricing law: never discount the price, only the arithmetic). Sell annuals from week 1 — cash de-risks the sprint long before MRR compounds.

The daily workflow (CAT, in order — no skipping ahead).

  1. 07:30 — Reply queue to zero. Every reply less than 24h old gets answered before anything else. Money before machine.
  2. 08:00 — Cold machine. Pull 30 leads (BATCH_CAP 30), QA each one (right person, right company, no dupes), confirm the 08:21 compose is queued. Caps live in scripts/outreach.py: DRIP_PER_RUN 5, DAILY_CAP 50/mailbox.
  3. 09:00 — Founder selling, 2 hours. Follow-ups, demos, trial check-ins (day 1/3/7 of every trial). No building in this block.
  4. 11:00 — Content batch. Owner non-negotiables: X (3 posts × 2 personas + replies), LinkedIn (3) — every link tracked (?src=). The press autopilot runs the scheduled rails (X, LinkedIn, Pinterest, Bluesky, Nostr, Whop — see the Press ledger); the owner covers replies and re-posts anything the witness log flags failed.
  5. 12:00 — Whop forum. One value post, answer every open thread, recruit affiliates (5 new/week — the pitch is the math: one Studio referral pays $184/mo for 12 months, $2,207 total).
  6. 14:00 — Long rails. dev.to (manual, per-persona — sprint floor is 3 posts/week); Pinterest top-up from cards.py; queue Bluesky/Nostr.
  7. 15:00 — Pipeline hygiene, 30 min. Move stages, kill dead leads, prep tomorrow's 30.
  8. Friday 15:00 — Weekly review (scoreboard below) instead of hygiene.

Lean mode: the same sprint in ~3h/day (switch after W1, not before).

Full mode above is ≈7h/day. Once every automation below has been green for 7 straight days, the same machine runs lean: ≈3h on normal days, ≈5h on Tue/Thu call days, Friday +review. Nothing is dropped — volume moves to machines, the owner keeps judgment. Run full mode in W1 so you learn what green looks like; switch to lean only when you can tell green from silent.

What the machines already carry (verified 2026-10-09): lead intake fills D1 twice daily (leads-hunt.yml 07:23/14:23 SAST); the 08:21 weekday compose queues the batch and posts its card (outreach.yml); replies are triaged 3×/day — opt-outs→DNC, bounces→dead, real replies→owner ping; the press autopilot publishes 4 slots/day, 7 days/week (press.yml, recent runs all green).

# Lean block Minutes

2 Cold QA: scan the auto-pulled batch, confirm the 08:21 card 15

— Call batches Tue/Thu (prospects take scheduled slots; async covers the gaps) +2h those days

Non-negotiables — never cut: <24h follow-up, daily cold QA, daily replies, daily forum, Friday scoreboard. Exception paths: intake short of 30 → owner tops up manually that morning (intake was deliberately shrunk 2026-10-09, so watch this); any autopilot run red → owner hand-posts that day's rails; a trial waiting on delivery jumps the whole queue — day-1 first-pack is the conversion lever. Banked time goes to delivery speed first, a third call batch second, never to product work (the feature freeze stands). Note: the bible's Press ledger reads the main-branch snapshot and lags — the live ledger commits to the press-state branch, and the Actions tab is the day-to-day truth.

The honest funnel note. 150 cold touches/week × 8 weeks ≈ 1,200 touches. At a 3% reply rate that is ~36 conversations → ~9 calls → ~3 closes from pure cold. Cold alone does NOT reach 22 — it feeds the pipe; founder selling, affiliates, referrals, and Discover close the gap. If cold is the only channel working by end of W3, the ladder is in danger: escalate to the Friday rules.

Closing rules.

  1. Follow-up inside 24 hours, always — speed is the entire edge.
  2. The trial aha-moment is the first pack delivered fast; the Whop review ask happens AT delivery, not later (reviews unlock Discover).
  3. Every quote: monthly first, annual second. Never discount the price, only the arithmetic.
  4. The affiliate rate is 30% recurring for 12 months — recruit on that math, never by cutting price.
  5. Every happy customer gets asked twice: a Whop review, and one referral name.
  6. No link ships without ?src= — untracked links make Fridays blind.

The Friday scoreboard (kill / scale). Track seven numbers: new paying (target: 3), cold reply %, trial→paid %, active affiliates, review count, MRR, cash collected. Then apply the rules: cold reply under 2% two weeks running → rewrite the opener AND change the list source; trial→paid under 15% → fix day-1 onboarding before chasing more traffic (there is no ad budget — fix onboarding); fewer than 5 active affiliates by end of W4 → double forum recruiting; any channel at ≥1 customer/week → double its time block next week; any channel at zero after two weeks → kill it and move the hours to the winner.

What can break this. (1) Building instead of selling — feature freeze for the full sprint: no product work unless a named deal needs it. (2) Zero public reviews — Discover stays locked; the review ask is part of delivery, not an afterthought. (3) The affiliate toggle still open (first-month vs 12-month is an owner setting) — decide in W1; this bible's pricing truth is 30% recurring for 12 months. (4) Slow first pack — trials that wait, churn; day-1 delivery is the conversion lever. (5) Untracked links — if ?src= is missing, the Friday review is guesswork.

What never leaves this building (reminders that outrank any playbook)

Nothing sends without a human tap - that is the product, so it is also the pitch. No invented stats, ever: beats are number-free; numbers live in the ledger and are dated. The demo is "free forever", never a "free trial" (the hosted trial is the 7-day one). One CTA per artifact. Two value posts per promo. The human is the hero.

No single board sees the whole market (1 day before fetch)

Every employer in the region spreads listings across a mix of national portals, niche sites and their own career pages. A search that stops at one source is a search that stops at a slice.

Board-specific habits — Large boards tend to post high-volume, entry-level roles on a daily cadence, while niche boards focus on specialised functions and update less frequently. Company pages often appear only when a vacancy is urgent. Recognising these patterns lets you allocate time where it matters.

Duplicate postings as a signal — When the same role appears on three or more boards, the market is telling you the position is real and time-sensitive. Treat duplicates as high-priority items, not as wasted effort.

Scheduling the sweep — The biggest operational leak is checking the same boards at random times. Build a repeatable schedule: morning run on the two national portals, mid-day scan of the top niche sites, afternoon check of company pages. Consistency turns a chaotic search into a predictable workflow.

Quality control for clients — Keep a log of each board visited, time spent and any duplicates flagged. Share that log with clients as proof of diligence; it turns hours into transparent value.

Brand impact — Delivering a full-market snapshot reinforces your practice's reputation for thoroughness. Clients notice the difference between a "we looked everywhere" report and a list that only reflects one board's feed.

Treat board coverage as a scheduling problem, not a data-collection problem. Align your daily routine with board habits, flag duplicates, log the process, and let the consistency speak for your brand.

Speed is a service you can sell (2 days)

Set a weekly response window and treat it like a service contract. Allocate a fixed slot - say two hours every Tuesday - to scan the selected public sources, score openings and draft replies. The promise is visible; work happens automatically, keeping client ledger clean and brand reliable.

Your caseload ceiling is a logistics number (3 days)

Read a job ad: 5 min; rewrite cover: 15 min; send: 3 min. Coaching: 30 min. Each new client adds 20 min to reading+rewrite, while coaching stays flat. Raise your limit by automating the non-judgment steps or using a tool - not by burning after hours.

The caps are the feature (Sep 23)

Most job hunt tools encourage high volume, treating applications as a numbers game. STPi operates differently. We build guardrails into the system, not bottlenecks, to prevent burnout and encourage focused effort.

Our approval gate, for instance, requires a human click before anything sends. This simple step prevents reactive submissions and ensures every application is deliberate. The 30-day cooldown on reapplying to the same role or employer serves a similar purpose, preventing over-eagerness and promoting strategic engagement.

These are not limitations; they are design choices. The goal is to make burnout unsendable, to enforce a sustainable pace. The free demo reflects this, allowing one candidate, five sends per UTC month, free forever. This core philosophy applies across all product tiers.

STPi focuses on quality over unchecked quantity, helping users manage the process rather than being overwhelmed by it.

We put a human approval gate inside a job application robot, on purpose (Sep 20)

Most job-hunt tools optimize the same thing: send more, faster, with AI-polished wording everywhere. We built the opposite trade on purpose and it is worth explaining why, because the reasoning matters even if you never touch our product.

A search has two very different halves. The boring eighty percent (reading listings, scoring fit against what a job description actually repeats, tailoring drafts, timing follow-ups, keeping a tracker honest) is language logistics, and it is fully automatable. The twenty percent that carries your name, your judgment, your voice in the room, is not, and the moment a tool sends that part unattended it stops being leverage and starts being liability.

So the machine we shipped, stpi, runs the first half on a schedule and hard-gates the second: every application sits behind an approval click, sends are spaced, daily drafts are capped, and a 30-day cooldown per employer is enforced in code, not policy. Burnout volume is not discouraged; it is physically unavailable. The caps run the same way in the free demo (one candidate, five sends per UTC month, free forever) as in the paid tiers, which start at thirty dollars because support costs money.

The open questions I would genuinely like this forum's opinion on: what should an approval gate refuse by default? Which two columns of an application tracker would you never give up? If the answers get good, they ship.
