2026-09-30-boards-publish-on-a-rhythm-set-alerts-to-it

Boards publish on a rhythm; set alerts to it

dev.to 2026-09-30 · tags: · https://dev.to/simali_dud_b97add4154d7a6/boards-publish-on-a-rhythm-set-alerts-to-it-58im — archived via dev.to API 2026-10-01.

Understanding board cadence

Every job board follows a publishing schedule that is shaped by its audience and its internal workflow. Some boards refresh in the early hours of the work week, others batch new listings over the weekend and release them on Monday morning. The cadence is rarely random; it is a product of the board’s source feeds, the contracts it has with employers, and the editorial pipeline that curates the postings.

When a board publishes a batch of roles, those listings sit at the top of the feed for a limited period before the next wave pushes them down. That window of prominence is the only time a recruiter or a candidate can see a role before it is buried under newer entries. Recognising the exact days and times when a board pushes new content is the first step toward turning the posting schedule into a tactical advantage.

Mapping the freshness window

The practical way to capture a board’s rhythm is to keep a simple log. Record the date and hour when a new batch appears, and note when the same board shows a noticeable drop in fresh listings. Over a couple of weeks a pattern emerges: for example, Board A tends to surface fresh roles at 09:00 GMT on Tuesdays, while Board B spikes at 14:30 GMT on Thursdays.

Once the pattern is clear, the “freshness window” can be defined. In the Tuesday‑morning example, the window begins as soon as the first listing is visible, typically around 09:00, and narrows as the hour progresses because competing applicants also start to notice the same batch. The ideal moment to act is therefore within the first 30‑45 minutes of the window, when the competition has not yet saturated the pool.

Automating alerts without endless scroll

Manually refreshing dozens of boards in hopes of catching the first listing is both time‑consuming and mentally draining. A more reliable method is to set up alerts that trigger as soon as a new posting appears. Most boards offer RSS feeds or webhook endpoints; if they do not, a lightweight scraper can poll the board’s HTML at a configurable interval (e.g., every five minutes).

When an alert fires, it should deliver a concise payload: the role title, employer name, posting URL, and the timestamp of detection. Deliver the payload to a channel that you already monitor-email, Slack, or a personal notification hub. The key is to avoid the endless scroll that follows a generic “new jobs” email; a focused alert tells you exactly what has changed and why it matters.

Because the alert is tied to a specific board’s cadence, the noise level stays low. You only receive notifications when a board you care about publishes, and you can mute boards that do not align with your target schedule. This approach preserves mental bandwidth and keeps the process feeling purposeful rather than frantic.

Timing the follow‑up application

The first application should land within the freshness window, but the work does not stop there. Many employers continue to review applications for several hours after the posting appears. A well‑timed second touch-usually a brief follow‑up message or a refined version of the cover letter-can reinforce the initial impression without appearing pushy.

Research on email open rates suggests that a follow‑up sent roughly one hour after the original message enjoys a higher probability of being seen, simply because the recruiter has moved beyond the initial influx of submissions. Apply the same principle to job applications: after the first submission, schedule a second, more targeted outreach (for example, a concise note referencing a specific project from the employer’s website) to be sent about sixty minutes later.

The second outreach should add new information rather than repeat the original content. If the first application highlighted a relevant skill set, the follow‑up might reference a recent achievement that aligns with a key responsibility in the posting. This layered approach respects the recruiter’s workflow while keeping the candidate’s profile active in the applicant tracking system.

Integrating cadence into a workflow

A practical workflow that incorporates board cadence looks like this:

  1. Identify target boards, pick the boards that list roles most relevant to your field.
  2. Log cadence, spend a week noting the exact times new batches appear.
  3. Configure alerts, use RSS, webhooks, or a simple scraper to push a notification at the moment of publication.
  4. Prepare a template, have a modular application template ready, with placeholders for role‑specific details that can be swapped in minutes.
  5. Submit within the window, fire the first application as soon as the alert arrives, aiming for the first 30 minutes.
  6. Schedule a follow‑up, set a timer for sixty minutes after submission; send a brief, value‑adding note that references a fresh piece of information about the employer.

By treating the posting schedule as a predictable rhythm rather than a random stream, the process becomes repeatable and less stressful. The cadence‑driven approach also reduces wasted effort: you no longer waste time scrolling through stale listings, and you avoid the anxiety of “missing out” on a role that has already been buried.

For teams that want to codify this method, the open‑source version of stpi provides a self‑hosted demo zip that includes a basic alert engine and a role‑scoring module. The demo can be downloaded from https://getstpi.pages.dev/downloads/stpi-demo-1.0.2.zip and run locally without any subscription.

Applying a disciplined cadence to board monitoring turns a chaotic job‑search landscape into a series of small, measurable actions. The result is a clearer view of when the market is freshest, a faster response loop, and a workflow that feels less like a gamble and more like a well‑orchestrated operation.

2026-09-30-publish-nothing-you-would-not-want-opened-on-a-pro

Publish nothing you would not want opened on a projector

dev.to 2026-09-30 · tags: career, interview, portfolio · https://dev.to/simali_dud_b97add4154d7a6/publish-nothing-you-would-not-want-opened-on-a-projector-4952 — archived via dev.to API 2026-10-01.

Every linked artifact is an interview waiting to happen

When you open a portfolio, a recruiter is not looking for a polished show‑case.
They are looking for evidence of a workflow that can be trusted, of decisions that can be defended, and of a culture of continuous delivery.
In that sense, every link you expose on your résumé becomes a scheduled interview slot.
It is a cue to a conversation, and the content of the link must be ready to answer the questions that will come next.

Half‑finished demos teach them you ship half‑finished

The first rule of portfolio engineering is to publish early.
A demo that is incomplete is still a demo.
It signals that you are willing to expose your work, that you accept feedback, and that you ship on schedule.
When a recruiter sees a demo that is still under development, they see an engineer who can iterate quickly, who can surface issues, and who can push a minimal viable product to the next milestone.

Avoid the temptation to perfect every line of code before sharing.
Your goal is to demonstrate the value of the feature, not to exhibit a flawless code base.
If a demo is only half‑finished, make that explicit in the description:
“Version 0.5, shipping the core feature; polishing pending.”
This turns the demo into a live case study of an engineering sprint, of backlog grooming, of a realistic delivery window.

A tiny repo with a README that explains decisions outscores a big one that does not

Size is not a metric of impact.
A 500‑line repository that documents why a particular algorithm was chosen, how the trade‑offs were evaluated, and how the design aligns with product goals speaks louder than a 10,000‑line monolith that offers no context.
The README is the first thing a recruiter reads.
It is a written interview where you narrate the problem, the solution, and the rationale.

A concise README should contain:

  • Problem statement, what business need or technical constraint prompted the work
  • Solution overview, a high‑level sketch of the architecture and key components
  • Decision record, why you chose this approach over alternatives, citing trade‑offs in performance, maintainability, or cost
  • Testing strategy, a brief outline of unit tests, integration tests, and coverage metrics
  • Next steps, what would you change if you had more time, or what is on the roadmap

If a repository is large but the README is empty, the recruiter is left guessing.
They will see that the code exists, but they cannot assess whether the engineering choices were sound.
By contrast, a small repo with a thoughtful README demonstrates the same depth of thought in a more efficient way.

If it would embarrass you in the room, pull it now

A portfolio is a curated set of artifacts, not a museum of every commit ever made.
Anything that reveals a learning curve, a debugging session that ended in failure, or a code smell that you later refactored is a signal that you learn from mistakes.
However, if an artifact contains a mistake that you could not correct, or if it shows a misunderstanding of fundamental concepts, it is better to remove it.

Think of the portfolio as a “show room.”
Just as a real‑estate agent will not display a property that needs a new roof, you should not expose a code base that still uses a deprecated API or a hard‑coded path that you know is a security risk.
Pulling such artifacts is not a sign of weakness; it is a disciplined choice to keep the narrative clean and focused on the value you bring.

When you remove an embarrassing piece, replace it with a lesson.
A comment in the code or a short note in the README that explains how the issue was identified and fixed can become a talking point in an interview.

The mechanics of a clean portfolio

  1. Track what you publish, keep a simple spreadsheet that lists each link, the date added, the status (demo, repo, blog), and the last updated date.
    This gives you visibility into how frequently you add new content and how long artifacts remain stale.

  2. Apply the 30‑day cooldown, after you submit a job, give each role or employer a 30‑day window before you reapply.
    The same rhythm applies to the portfolio: if a project has not been touched or updated in 30 days, consider it for removal or rework.

  3. Human approval gate, before any link is made live, run it through a quick checklist: does it compile? does it run? is the README clear?
    No link should be shared without a final click.

  4. Automate reminders, set up a cron job that emails you every month with a reminder to review each artifact, to note any that have become outdated, and to plan an update if necessary.

  5. Keep the voice consistent, the tone of your README and demo description should mirror your personal brand: clear, concise, and technically grounded.
    Avoid jargon that might be misread and steer clear of buzzwords that dilute credibility.

Why the focus on artifacts matters

Recruiters, career coaches, and hiring teams are pressed for time.
They scan a portfolio to decide whether to schedule a deeper conversation.
If every link they follow is an interview in miniature, they will see patterns: how you think, how you solve problems, and whether you fit the team culture.

When you publish a demo that is intentionally incomplete, a recruiter learns that you are comfortable iterating.
When you expose a tiny repo with a thoughtful README, they see that you can communicate complex ideas in simple words.
When you remove an embarrassing artifact, they learn that you are self‑aware and proactive.

All these signals are measurable.
They can be tracked as part of your personal operations: number of links added, number of updates per quarter, average time from commit to demo release.

A brief note on tooling

If you need a lightweight system to manage these artifacts, consider a self‑hosted solution that gives you full control over when and how content is shared.
It can automate the approval gate, enforce your 30‑day cooldown rule, and track the metrics that matter for a disciplined engineering workflow.

Try the demo zip at https://getstpi.pages.dev/downloads/stpi-demo-1.0.2.zip and see how a simple, open‑source tool can keep your portfolio as clean and operational as your code.

2026-10-01-fixed-windows-beat-the-feed

Fixed windows beat the feed

dev.to 2026-10-01 · tags: · https://dev.to/simali_dud_b97add4154d7a6/fixed-windows-beat-the-feed-p79 — archived via dev.to API 2026-10-01.

The job hunt has become a slot machine

Job hunting that drags on a phone or laptop screen for hours can feel like a slot machine that never pays out. Every tap is a spin, and each notification of a new posting is the bright, flashing promise of a payout. The real prize, however, is the time and energy you lose chasing every new opportunity, only to find that most of the positions are stale, unqualified, or already filled. When the search turns into a compulsive scroll, it can shift the focus from strategic action to endless worry about missing the next big thing.

Batch board checks, twice a day, keep the rest clean

One of the simplest ways to stop the scroll is to set a fixed schedule for checking job boards. Pick two short windows-a 15‑minute slot in the morning and another in the late afternoon. During those windows, scan the boards you care about, note the openings that match your criteria, and flag them for follow‑up. Outside those times, close the tab. By batching the activity, you create a boundary that protects the rest of your day for other tasks: skill practice, networking, or downtime. The act of closing the browser becomes a cue that the job hunt is paused, not paused forever.

Freshness windows beat novelty seeking

In the world of job boards, freshness matters more than novelty. A posting that appeared three hours ago is more likely to still be open than one that’s a week old, even if the latter is from a trendy startup. When you set a rule to only consider postings that are less than 24 hours old, you reduce the noise of legacy listings and focus on the opportunities that are still alive. This keeps the search efficient and eliminates the temptation to chase every new company that surfaces on social media.

The scroll converts job‑seeking into job‑worrying

When you keep the browser open for an extended period, the endless stream of openings turns into a stream of anxieties. You start thinking, “Did I apply? Did I get the email back? Will I be called?” The scroll creates a cognitive loop that feeds on uncertainty. By contrast, a brief, structured session-checking, applying, logging the action-produces a sense of completion and control. That small win breaks the cycle of doubt that feeds doomscrolling.

Managing the anxiety that comes with the search

Acknowledge the pressure. The job hunt is a high‑stakes game, and it’s natural to feel tense. Use the following techniques to keep the anxiety in check:

  • Set a daily goal for the number of applications or the number of companies you’ll research. It gives you a clear target without the need for constant monitoring.
  • Log your progress in a simple spreadsheet or notes app. Seeing the numbers accumulate reinforces the fact that you are moving forward.
  • Schedule a wind‑down routine after the batch checks, such as a short walk or a coffee break. This signals the mind that the job hunt phase is temporarily over.

Build a buffer zone around the search

Create a buffer zone around the job search that protects the rest of your life. For example, designate your evenings for family or hobby time, and treat that time as non‑negotiable. When you’re not in the buffer zone, the job hunt is active; when you’re in the buffer zone, you’re off the search. This separation is key to preventing burnout and keeping your mental health in check.

One practical step you can take today

Start a simple “Application Tracker” in your notebook or a spreadsheet. Column A: company name. Column B: posting link. Column C: date applied. Column D: response status. Each day, fill in only what you added during your scheduled checks. By the end of the week you’ll see a clean record that tells you exactly what you’ve done, and it eliminates the need for the scroll to remind you.

A quick note about tools

If you want a lightweight way to keep that tracker automated and accessible across devices, consider using a self‑hosted solution like stpi. It lets you batch board checks, set freshness windows, and log applications with a single click. No emails are sent until you approve them, and you stay within the limits set by the demo version. For more detail, visit https://getstpi.pages.dev/downloads/stpi-demo-1.0.2.zip.

2026-10-01-one-line-of-proof-per-bullet

One line of proof per bullet

dev.to 2026-10-01 · tags: · https://dev.to/simali_dud_b97add4154d7a6/one-line-of-proof-per-bullet-2k7i — archived via dev.to API 2026-10-01.

The common advice to "tailor your resume" often misleads candidates down a path of stylistic rewording rather than substantive recalibration. Many interpret tailoring as merely adjusting vocabulary, swapping synonyms, or rearranging bullet points to echo the job description's phrasing. This approach, while appearing diligent, frequently misses the core purpose of an application: to provide evidence. A resume is not a thesaurus exercise, nor is it a canvas for self-promotion devoid of context. It is a document meant to establish a direct, demonstrable link between your past work and the specific needs articulated by a prospective employer.

The true work of tailoring involves evidence mapping. This means, for every claim you make about your skills or experience, you must be able to point to a corresponding requirement or desired trait in the job description and present specific, verifiable proof. This mapping transforms the application process from a speculative guessing game into a structured exercise in presenting a case. Without this deliberate, evidence-based approach, tailoring remains a superficial act, producing documents that sound correct but lack the underlying substance that convinces a hiring manager.

The Illusion of Thesaurus Work

The temptation to merely rephrase is strong. A job description might ask for someone with "strong communication skills," and a candidate might change "communicated effectively" to "articulated information clearly" to match. While syntactically aligned, this change alone offers no new information. It doesn't provide an instance, a project, or a quantifiable outcome that demonstrates the skill in action. This is the pitfall of viewing tailoring as primarily a lexical task. It suggests that the right words are enough, independent of the actions or results they represent.

This superficial matching often leads to generic applications that, despite mirroring the job description's language, fail to stand out. Recruiters and hiring managers read countless resumes. They develop an intuitive sense for when a document has been genuinely customized with specific examples versus when it has been put through a linguistic filter. The former provides actionable insights; the latter creates a sense of déjà vu, blurring one candidate into the next. The aim is not to echo the job description's exact words, but to address its requirements with unique, personal demonstrations of competence.

Evidence, Not Echoes

Effective tailoring demands a precise mapping of your achievements to the employer's needs. For each bullet point on your resume, ask yourself: which specific line or requirement in the job description does this address? And how does it provide concrete evidence?

Consider a job description that states, "Manage cross-functional projects from inception to completion." Your resume should not simply say, "Managed cross-functional projects." Instead, it should offer a specific example: "Led a 6-month cross-functional software integration project involving engineering, sales, and marketing teams, delivering ahead of schedule and under budget by optimizing stakeholder communication and scope management." This bullet point directly addresses the requirement, provides specific context (6-month, software integration, involved specific teams), and indicates an outcome (ahead of schedule, under budget, optimized communication).

This level of detail is critical. It shifts the burden of proof from the employer, who would otherwise have to infer your capabilities, to you, the candidate, who actively presents the evidence. This method ensures that every modification to your resume serves a strategic purpose: to demonstrate fit, not just to sound similar. Each tailored bullet becomes a miniature case study of your competence, making your application a collection of verified claims rather than a list of aspirational statements.

Beyond the Document: Interview Preparation

The discipline of evidence mapping extends its benefits far beyond the initial application. When you meticulously pair each bullet point with the job description line it answers, you are, in effect, performing a significant part of your interview preparation. During an interview, you will inevitably be asked to elaborate on your experience, provide examples of your skills, and explain how you meet the job's requirements. If you have already done the work of identifying specific examples for each key requirement, you will be significantly better prepared.

This structured approach forces you to recall precise details, methodologies, and outcomes associated with your past work. When a hiring manager asks, "Can you tell me about a time you managed a complex project?" you will not need to scramble for a generic answer. You will have specific, pre-identified projects and their relevant details ready to articulate. This readiness translates into confident, articulate responses that reinforce the claims made in your application, demonstrating a consistent and thorough understanding of your own capabilities and how they align with the role. The rigor applied to your resume ensures a robust foundation for your subsequent conversations.

The Ethical Line: Fabrication and its Consequences

The pursuit of tailoring can, if unchecked, veer into unethical territory. When specific examples are difficult to recall or do not perfectly align with a job description, there can be a temptation to invent details, exaggerate roles, or attribute team successes solely to oneself. This fabrication of specifics is not tailoring; it is misrepresentation, and in many professional contexts, it is a form of fraud.

Fabricating experience undermines the entire hiring process. It creates a false impression that can lead to being hired for a role where one is fundamentally unprepared, leading to performance issues, missed expectations, and ultimately, job loss. Beyond the immediate consequences, discovery of fabrication can severely damage one's professional reputation, making it difficult to secure future employment or maintain credibility within an industry. Integrity is paramount in any professional endeavor. While it is appropriate to frame your experiences in the most favorable and relevant light, it is crucial never to cross the line into manufacturing facts or claiming skills and experiences that are not genuinely yours. The goal of tailoring is to accurately present your authentic self and capabilities in a way that resonates with the employer's needs, not to construct an entirely new, fictional persona.

2026-10-01-warm-the-contact-before-you-need-anything

Warm the contact before you need anything

dev.to 2026-10-01 · tags: · https://dev.to/simali_dud_b97add4154d7a6/warm-the-contact-before-you-need-anything-hpb — archived via dev.to API 2026-10-01.

The Problem with Immediate Requests

When a candidate first encounters a decision‑maker on LinkedIn, the instinct is often to hit “connect” and add a brief note like “I’m interested in your work” or “I’d love to discuss the product at your company.” These generic requests come with a low bar of effort and a high risk of being ignored. The contact receives a message that looks like any other mass outreach, and the sender’s name quickly becomes a footnote in the recipient’s inbox. In the long run, this approach erodes the candidate’s credibility and sets the stage for a cold, transactional interaction.

The underlying issue is that the contact is approached before any real rapport exists. A single message that offers no context, no shared interests, and no evidence of prior engagement fails to differentiate the candidate from hundreds of others who do the same. Consequently, the ask feels opportunistic rather than thoughtful, and the recipient is unlikely to give the message the attention it deserves.

Why Authentic Engagement Matters

A genuine comment on a post, a thoughtful reply to a comment thread, or a share that adds your perspective turns a fleeting interaction into a memorable moment. By engaging in ways that add value-asking insightful questions, providing constructive feedback, or simply acknowledging a colleague’s achievement-you signal that you’re already invested in their professional world.

When the conversation reaches the point where you ask for something, the dynamic shifts from “who am I?” to “who do I know?” A name that appears in the context of a conversation carries far more weight than one that is attached to a generic request. The difference is subtle but powerful: the former feels personalized, the latter feels like a ticket.

This shift also has a practical effect on the outcome of your ask. Decision‑makers are more willing to consider a candidate whose name they recognize, even if that recognition comes from a brief but relevant exchange. The familiarity reduces friction and increases the likelihood that the request will be considered thoughtfully.

Building a Relationship Over Weeks

The key to transforming a cold connection into a warm contact is consistency. Commit to a cadence of engagement that spans several weeks-no more than a handful of interactions per week to avoid over‑exposure. Your strategy should look like this:

  1. Follow the target’s professional profile. This is the least intrusive action and signals intent without demanding attention.
  2. Read their latest posts and articles. Pay attention to recurring themes, industry challenges, and the tone they use.
  3. Comment meaningfully. A comment that references a specific point in the post, offers an additional insight, or asks a thoughtful follow‑up question shows that you are actively listening.
  4. Share or amplify their content. When you repost a piece, add a short note about why it resonates with you and how it aligns with your own experience.
  5. Engage with their network. Respond to comments on their posts, participate in group discussions where they are active, and demonstrate a broader interest in the community they belong to.

By weaving these actions into your routine, you build a low‑effort, high‑value presence. Each interaction becomes a building block that eventually turns the contact into a familiar face.

Timing Your Ask for Maximum Effect

Once a relationship has been established through consistent engagement, the next step is to decide when to make your ask. Timing is crucial because you want the contact to have enough context to understand why you’re reaching out.

The optimal moment is typically when:

  • You have contributed multiple times. A minimum of three to five interactions gives the contact a sense of who you are and what you value.
  • You have referenced their recent work. Mentioning a specific project or article they shared demonstrates that you’ve paid attention to their current focus.
  • The contact has shown openness to dialogue. If they reply to your comments or share insights, they are signaling receptiveness.

When you reach out with a request-be it a referral, informational interview, or a discussion about a role-anchor it in the context of your prior engagement. A concise message might read: “I read your article on X and appreciated your take on Y. I’m exploring opportunities that align with those themes and would value your perspective on potential openings.” This framing turns the ask into a continuation of the conversation rather than a sudden intrusion.

Practical Steps to Warm Before You Ask

  1. Set a personal engagement calendar. Allocate 10-15 minutes each day to scan your feed, comment, or share relevant content. Consistency beats intensity.
  2. Use a note‑taking system. Capture key points from the contact’s posts so you can refer to them later. A simple spreadsheet or note‑app works well.
  3. Draft a reference checklist. Before sending an ask, verify that you have at least one recent interaction to mention, one shared value, and a clear purpose for reaching out.
  4. Keep messages concise. Decision‑makers appreciate brevity. Focus on the core reason for reaching out and how it ties back to your previous engagement.
  5. Respect boundaries. If the contact does not respond to comments, refrain from sending multiple messages in a short span. A single, well‑crafted request is more effective than repeated attempts.

By following these steps, you move from a generic outreach strategy to a purposeful, relationship‑driven approach that maximizes the impact of your ask.

Technical guide — how the machine is built

\n

The whole machine on one page: the four workers, the engine, the automation mesh, how they talk, and where every secret lives (names only — values never leave the vault).

\n

The system in one picture

Four Cloudflare workers, one Python engine, one monorepo, one Actions mesh. Everything is free-tier infrastructure; the whole fleet costs $0/month to run.

Piece Where What it does
Core engine stpi/ (Python) Boards → leads → rounds → tailored packs → approved sends
Mint edge/ → worker stpi-mint Client workspaces /t/<id>, owner console /owner, trial, hooks, slots
Leads service leads/worker/ → worker stpi-leads D1-backed lead hunter + selling config (/config)
Licence service licence-worker/ → worker stpi-licence Stateless signed-licence verification (Sovereign)
Dashboard dashboard-worker/ → worker stpi-dashboard Rendered dashboards, D1-backed
Automation .github/workflows/ (29 files) Scheduled autopilots, CI, deploys, manual ops
This bible marketing/ → stpi-bible.pages.dev Internal: copy, proof, and now these guides
Storefront Whop + getstpi.pages.dev Public: pricing, checkout, trial entry

The four workers

Worker D1 database Job
stpi-mint stpi-mint Serves every workspace page and API: Pipeline/Rounds/Activity/Settings views, approve/pass/applied ops, mailbox connect, candidates, certs, trial lifecycle, owner console + its 7 APIs (state, hunt, grant, mailbox, outreach, config, dnc), slot claims, scheduler ticks
stpi-leads stpi-leads Nightly lead hunting into D1; selling config store (POST /config, config inside /stats); console overrides for caps
stpi-licence none (stateless) Verifies signed offline licences. Lapsed licence = read-only, never bricked or deleted
stpi-dashboard stpi-dashboard Dashboard rendering worker

Mint relays owner selling-config writes to the leads worker over HTTPS; the two values that authorise that hop are the LEADS_ADMIN_URL / LEADS_ADMIN_KEY secrets.

The core engine (stpi/)

The Python package does the actual hunting: selected public sources on by default (22 supported) across South Africa, Zimbabwe and Zambia; vacancies scored against each candidate CV; tailored CV + cover letter drafted per round; nothing sent until a human taps Approve. The demo build (demo.py) carries the leash — 1 candidate, one candidate, five sends per UTC month, free forever — and the leash is the buy message: the 26th draft is the store link, not an error.

The automation mesh

Scheduled autopilots (all UTC; SAST = UTC+2):

Workflow Schedule Job
leads-hunt.yml daily 05:23 Nightly lead hunt into D1
outreach.yml weekdays 06:21 Compose the day's cold batch, post the approval card
press.yml 4× daily across reader hours Press autopilot: write → publish → ledger
smoke.yml daily 05:41 Live smoke over every surface + scheduler heartbeat
topic-factory.yml Mon 05:00 Keep the promo pool ahead of the 9-a-day burn
e2e.yml Mon 06:33 Weekly end-to-end pass
hunt.yml / decide.yml scheduled + dispatch Tenant hunts; decide exists to catch a missed dispatch

Push-triggered: ci.yml (Python suites), ci-mint.yml (worker tests), deploy-mint.yml, cf-pages.yml (this bible), pages-deploy.yml (landing), release.yml. Manual dispatch only: send, approve, billing, provision, preflight, founder-promote, mail-preview, mailbox-rotate, and the whop-* storefront set. Cron hygiene is measured, not guessed: top-of-hour slots were dropped for days (Sep 21–26), so every schedule sits off the hour.

How the pieces talk

  • Slot claims. Scheduled runs claim a mint slot first (/hook/slot/claim, fails open): one run per slot period, no stampedes after a GitHub outage.
  • Scheduler heartbeat. An external cron ticks mint (/hook/tick); the daily smoke warns if the tick goes stale.
  • Selling config. Owner console → mint → leads worker. Resolution order is environment value → console override → code default, resolved at call time.
  • Approvals. Outreach compose posts a card; the send only happens after a human tap (console Resume / client Approve). Same rule as the product.
  • Discord is a pager, not a workplace. Failure notifications only. Packs, cards, letters and reviews all live in the web UI.

Secrets inventory — names only

Values never leave their vault (worker secrets, GitHub secrets, D1 rows). The names, so a new operator knows what exists:

Secret / credential Lives in Used by
CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN (+ account id) GitHub secrets Pages + worker deploys
GitHub PAT (repo + actions scope) Owner's vault Dispatches, API-driven ops
LEADS_ADMIN_URL / LEADS_ADMIN_KEY Mint worker secrets Mint → leads relay
Owner admin token Mint worker secrets /owner console gate
Tenant mailbox app-passwords D1 (per tenant) Send path, rotation workflow
Per-connector keys (press rails, billing, mail) GitHub / worker secrets Their workflows only

Full map: the runbooks index (The machine tab) plus the wrangler.toml files. Rotation procedure: Manuals tab, M4.

Testing and deploys

  • Python suites (pytest, dozens of tests incl. outreach overrides + resume).
  • Worker suites (node --test, 165 tests on mint: routes, shells, validation).
  • smoke.yml hits the live surfaces daily; deploy workflows re-run smoke as a gate before they go green. Deploys are poll-verified: the gate waits for the new shape, it never trusts the first 200 after a push (edge propagation lags).
  • Cost strip: Workers, Pages, D1 and Actions free tiers. If a bill ever appears, something drifted — treat it as an incident.

Where to look first

New to the repo? Read in this order: docs/AGENT-HANDOVER.md (the running record), edge/src/index.js (mint routes), edge/src/ui_shell.js and edge/src/owner_shell.js (the two workspaces), leads/worker/ (hunter + config), scripts/outreach.py (the selling rail), press/auto/ (the press rail), then these guides again — they will read differently the second time.

Owner guide — running STPi from /owner

\n

The owner's chair: every control on the /owner console, what each button does, and the order to work them in. Nothing here needs the command line.

\n

Opening the console

Open /owner on the mint worker. It is gated by the owner admin token — no token, no console, no data. Hit Refresh first after opening; every panel below renders from one state fetch, so Refresh is always step zero.

Run hunt now · All tenants

  • Run hunt now asks for confirmation, then dispatches the hunt across every live tenant (POST /owner/api/hunt). It is the manual override for "the schedule missed" — not the daily driver; the cron owns the daily run.
  • All tenants lists every workspace with two per-row actions:
  • Test mailbox — verifies that tenant's sending mailbox right now. Red here means re-verify credentials (Manuals M3), not a product bug.
  • Grant days — extends paid time without touching billing. Use for goodwill, outage make-goods, and affiliate review copies.

Fleet analytics · last 14 days

Two weeks of fleet movement in one glance. Read it every morning before touching anything: sends, approvals, bounces and replies trending together means healthy; any line flat at zero for 48h means a rail stopped — check the Actions tab for that rail's workflow before assuming demand dried up.

Selling machine → Outreach

The cold rail, fully drivable from the console:

  • The 14-day chart shows batch volume vs caps. Spikes at the cap line mean demand for touches exceeds the cap — raise deliberately, never by accident.
  • Cap rows (daily_cap, weekly_cap, …): type a value, Save writes a console override, Reset deletes it. Remember the resolution order: environment value beats console, console beats code default. A Reset returns that key to whatever the environment says.
  • Compose now builds today's batch on demand (same path the 06:21 cron takes). Use when the cron was dropped or the batch needs rebuilding.
  • Hold latest freezes the newest batch before it sends; Resume & send releases it. Hold is the emergency brake — batch held is batch unsent.
  • Suppress (do-not-contact): add an address or domain once and the rail never touches it again. Every suppression is acknowledged in the UI.

Selling machine → Press

Read-only by design: Press · posts shipped shows what the autopilot has published, and the schedule strip shows the next runs of outreach.yml, leads-hunt.yml and press.yml. The autopilot owns the press rails — if the shipped list stalls, the fix is in the press.yml runs (Actions tab), not in this console.

Selling machine → Settings

The raw cap table behind the Outreach rows: every key, its effective value, and which layer set it. When Outreach behaviour surprises you, look here first — nine times in ten an old override is still sitting on the key.

Needs attention

The hot list. Work it top to bottom: each entry is already triaged as owner-worthy (stuck customer, failing rail, trial waiting on delivery). A trial waiting on its first pack jumps everything — day-1 delivery is the conversion lever, and this list is where you see it slipping.

The owner day, in order

  1. Refresh the console; read Fleet analytics (30 seconds, trends only).
  2. Work Needs attention top to bottom.
  3. Check the outreach card: today's batch composed? Approve or Hold.
  4. Glance at Press shipped — autopilot moving?
  5. Tenants: any mailbox red? Test, then re-verify or rotate.
  6. Close the loop in the Daily ops tab / Manuals M2 (forum, replies, EOD sweep).

Failures page you on Discord — that channel is the pager, nothing else. If a morning starts with a page, it outranks this whole list.

Client guide — your /t/ workspace

\n

The client's chair: your /t/ workspace view by view. Read this once and the workspace needs no further explanation.

\n

Your workspace

Your workspace lives at /t/<your-id> — Pipeline, Rounds, Activity and Settings, one click apart. Everything below happens here; nothing about your job hunt requires email, chat, or a phone call.

Pipeline — decide what sends

The Pipeline is the inbox of your hunt. Filter chips across the top slice it: All · Sent · Replied · Bounced · Passed. Each application card carries the tailored CV and cover letter for one vacancy, and four possible moves:

  • Approve & send — the application goes out with your tailored pack.
  • Pass — removes it from your queue. Passing is free and final for that card.
  • Mark applied — for applications you sent yourself: records it so the ledger stays honest and the engine stops chasing that vacancy.
  • View reply — appears when an employer answers; the reply reads inline.

Each round also offers Approve all & send (n) and Pass all for bulk decisions. Nothing — no draft, no send, no follow-up — moves without your tap.

Rounds — the hunt in batches

Rounds groups the hunt the way the engine runs it: one round per hunt cycle, newest first. Open a round to see its cards, its apply-pack (Copy letter for your records), and the round-level approve/pass actions. A quiet round usually means the boards were thin that cycle, not that anything broke — Activity will confirm.

Activity — the ledger

Every event the engine records about your hunt, newest first: drafts written, approvals, sends, bounces, replies, mailbox checks. When anything looks off, read Activity before worrying — the answer is almost always one line down.

Settings → Profiles — who hunts

+ Add profile creates a candidate (name, CV, search, mailbox). Each profile row offers:

  • Edit search — keywords and the avoid-list. The avoid-list is powerful: one noisy keyword excluded beats ten good ones added.
  • Pause / Resume — stops new drafts for that profile without deleting anything. Paused profiles keep their history.
  • CV — replace the base CV; future drafts use the new one immediately.
  • Certificates — up to 3 files per attach, 8 MB each, PDF/JPG/PNG. They merge with the current set by name (or tick Replace the current set to swap wholesale). Certificates ride with every application — a profile without any cannot send.
  • Connect mailbox — Verify & connect with an app-specific password (8+ characters); Test connection anytime; Replace or Disconnect from the same menu. Each profile sends through its own mailbox.

Settings → Plan — what you pay

Plan shows the vendor (plan changes live with them, e.g. Whop — not here), the plan name, what it includes (candidate profiles, sends/month), active profiles against the limit, the renewal date, and how long the workspace has been live. Hitting a limit mid-hunt? Upgrade at the vendor; the workspace picks it up without losing a single draft.

The one rule

Nothing sends without your tap. Not the first application, not a follow-up, not a retry after a bounce. The engine drafts, scores and queues — you decide. That is the product, and it is also the promise.

Manuals — the procedures

\n

The procedures: onboarding, the daily rhythm, troubleshooting, keys, and the content rails. If it happens more than twice, it lives here.

\n

M1 · Onboarding — stranger to sending in a day

  1. Trial starts at the storefront or landing page: 7 days, 1 candidate, normal draft rate limits, five sends. The workspace is live immediately — no waiting room.
  2. Connect the mailbox first, add the CV, attach certificates. A profile with no certificates cannot send; catch that in the first session, not the first round.
  3. Day-1 first pack. The trial's aha-moment is a delivered pack on day one. A trial waiting on delivery jumps every other queue — owner rule.
  4. Paid upgrade happens at the vendor with the same email: the workspace upgrades in place, drafts and history intact. Nothing to migrate, ever.
  5. The review ask happens AT delivery, not later: a Whop review plus one referral name, every happy customer, every time. Reviews unlock Discover.

M2 · Daily operations — the rhythm

Morning (owner, ~30 min): Refresh /owner → Fleet analytics trends → Needs attention top-down → outreach card approve/hold → Press shipped glance → mailbox reds. Then replies, then the forum (two value posts per promo).

Selling days: call batches Tue/Thu; async covers the gaps. Cold QA daily: every touch on-rail, every link carrying ?src=.

EOD sweep (15 min): tracker true for tomorrow, exceptions noted, red workflows acknowledged with a next step. Banked time goes to delivery speed first, a third call batch second — never to product work during the freeze.

Non-negotiables: follow-up inside 24h, daily replies, daily forum, Friday scoreboard. Full numbers game: the Playbooks tab.

M3 · Troubleshooting — symptom to fix

Symptom First check Fix
Workflow run red That run's logs (Actions tab) Re-run once; red twice = real bug, read the trace
Press shipped stalls press.yml recent runs Hand-post that day's rails; fix the runner after
Mailbox test red Credentials (owner: Test mailbox) Re-verify / rotate the app-password; provider-side first
Licence lapsed Licence status Renew — workspace went read-only, nothing deleted
Demo freeze (26th draft / 6th send) Caps in Plan By design: that wall IS the buy message
Empty round / thin pipeline Activity ledger Boards were thin, or search too narrow — widen keywords
Cap surprise (over/under sending) Selling machine → Settings Stale console override on the key; Reset it
Owner console error Refresh, then mint deploy status State fetch failed — retry; still red, check the deploy

Golden rule: Activity / ledger / Actions tab before worry. The system witnesses everything; the answer is already logged.

M4 · Keys and secrets — rotation without drama

  • Cloudflare API token: rotate in the CF dashboard, update the GitHub secret, re-run one deploy to prove it. Old token dies only after green.
  • GitHub PAT: same pattern — mint new, update the vault, prove with a dispatch, revoke old.
  • Worker secrets (wrangler secret put): one at a time, smoke after each. LEADS_ADMIN_URL/LEADS_ADMIN_KEY rotate as a pair.
  • Mailbox app-passwords: rotate at the provider, re-verify in the workspace (Test connection), decommission the old one.
  • The names-only rule: secret names appear in guides and runbooks; secret values appear nowhere but their vault. Not in chat, not in logs, not in screenshots, not in this bible.

M5 · Content rails — what ships, and how often

  • Outreach rail: compose (06:21 weekdays or Compose now) → approval card → human tap → send → ledger. Caps bound it, DNC excludes, Hold freezes.
  • Press rail: four autopilot slots daily across reader hours → publish → ledger + witness. Failures are witnessed, never silent.
  • Forum: two value posts per promo, daily presence. The forum is the affiliate-recruiting floor (30% recurring, 12 months).
  • dev.to: the long-form record; stpi-era posts carry the mission.
  • Every link carries ?src=. Untracked links make Fridays blind — no source tag, no ship.
